subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 68-year-old man presents with painless jaundice, dark urine, and pale stools. He has lost 8 kg over 3 months. Physical examination reveals a distended, nontender gallbladder. Serum CA 19-9 is markedly elevated.
question: Which of the following best explains the gallbladder finding?

options.text: Gallstone obstruction of the cystic duct causing acute cholecystitis
Chronic cholecystitis producing a fibrotic, shrunken gallbladder
Primary gallbladder adenocarcinoma arising in a porcelain gallbladder
Common bile duct obstruction by a pancreatic head tumor (Courvoisier sign)
Choledocholithiasis with ascending cholangitis

explanation_correct: Tumors of the pancreatic head, usually ductal adenocarcinoma, can obstruct the common bile duct, producing an enlarged nontender gallbladder with jaundice; this is Courvoisier sign. Pancreatic adenocarcinoma is associated with CA 19-9, with CEA also elevated but less specific. It often presents with abdominal pain radiating to the back, weight loss from malabsorption and anorexia, and obstructive jaundice. The tumor is very aggressive and is often metastatic at presentation.

explanation_incorrect.A: Cystic duct obstruction by a stone produces a tender, inflamed gallbladder with fever and a positive Murphy sign, not a painlessly distended one.
explanation_incorrect.B: Chronic cholecystitis produces a fibrotic, often shrunken gallbladder rather than the distended nontender gallbladder of malignant bile duct obstruction.
explanation_incorrect.C: Porcelain gallbladder is a calcified gallbladder from chronic cholecystitis with increased gallbladder cancer risk; it does not explain this classic painless jaundice with a distended gallbladder.
explanation_incorrect.E: Choledocholithiasis typically causes painful jaundice with cholestatic enzymes, and cholangitis adds fever, not a nontender distended gallbladder.

educationalObjective: A pancreatic head tumor obstructing the common bile duct causes painless jaundice with a palpable nontender gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) and elevated CA 19-9.
source: Generated from 9. Gastrointestinal.pdf - Pharmacology: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 71-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history presents with weight loss and painless jaundice. CT shows a mass in the head of the pancreas. Family history is notable for diabetes but not for pancreatic cancer.
question: Which genomic abnormality is most commonly associated with this tumor?

options.text: Activating KRAS mutation
Inactivating ATP7B mutation
Germline RET loss-of-function mutation
E-cadherin (CDH1) mutation
HFE gene mutation

explanation_correct: The most common genomic abnormality in pancreatic adenocarcinoma is an activating KRAS mutation. This very aggressive ductal tumor is often metastatic at presentation, with average survival of about one year after diagnosis. Tobacco smoking is the strongest risk factor, which fits this patient's heavy smoking history. Tumors in the pancreatic head lead to obstructive jaundice and are associated with CA 19-9.

explanation_incorrect.B: ATP7B mutation causes Wilson disease with impaired copper excretion, Kayser-Fleischer rings, and hepatic or neurologic disease.
explanation_incorrect.C: RET loss-of-function mutation causes Hirschsprung disease, a congenital aganglionic megacolon, not a pancreatic ductal tumor.
explanation_incorrect.D: E-cadherin mutation is associated with diffuse gastric adenocarcinoma and signet ring cells with linitis plastica.
explanation_incorrect.E: HFE mutation causes hereditary hemochromatosis with iron overload, cirrhosis, diabetes, and skin pigmentation.

educationalObjective: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma most commonly carries an activating KRAS mutation and has tobacco smoking as its strongest risk factor.
source: Generated from 9. Gastrointestinal.pdf - Pharmacology: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 66-year-old woman is evaluated for a 3-month history of epigastric pain radiating to the back and 10 kg weight loss. She has developed tender, reddened cord-like areas over both lower extremities that migrate over weeks. Imaging shows a pancreatic head mass with liver metastases.
question: Which of the following best describes this paraneoplastic manifestation?

options.text: Acanthosis nigricans associated with intestinal gastric adenocarcinoma
Virchow node metastasis from gastric cancer
Sister Mary Joseph nodule from gastric adenocarcinoma
Erythema nodosum from Crohn disease
Migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome) associated with pancreatic adenocarcinoma

explanation_correct: Migratory thrombophlebitis presents as redness and tenderness on palpation of the extremities and is known as Trousseau syndrome when associated with pancreatic adenocarcinoma. It is one of the classic presentations of this tumor along with abdominal pain radiating to the back, weight loss from malabsorption and anorexia, and obstructive jaundice with a palpable nontender gallbladder. These tumors arise from pancreatic ducts, are frequently metastatic at diagnosis, and carry a poor prognosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Acanthosis nigricans is a hyperpigmented skin finding linked to intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma, not a migratory thrombotic process.
explanation_incorrect.B: Virchow node refers to metastasis to the left supraclavicular lymph node, classically from gastric cancer, not to tender migratory cords on the legs.
explanation_incorrect.C: Sister Mary Joseph nodule is a subcutaneous periumbilical metastasis, most often from gastric adenocarcinoma.
explanation_incorrect.D: Erythema nodosum produces tender subcutaneous nodules in Crohn disease and other conditions but does not migrate as thrombophlebitis does.

educationalObjective: Migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome) is a classic paraneoplastic sign of pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
source: Generated from 9. Gastrointestinal.pdf - Pharmacology: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 70-year-old man with new painless jaundice and weight loss is found to have a pancreatic head mass. His clinician plans to follow his response to chemotherapy with a serum tumor marker.
question: Which tumor marker is most appropriate, and how does it compare with CEA?

options.text: CA 19-9; it is less specific than CEA for pancreatic cancer
CA 125; it is more specific than CEA for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
CA 19-9; it is associated with pancreatic adenocarcinoma, whereas CEA is less specific
AFP; it is the preferred marker for pancreatic ductal tumors
PSA; it is elevated in metastatic pancreatic disease

explanation_correct: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma is associated with the CA 19-9 tumor marker. CEA can also be elevated in this cancer but is less specific, so CA 19-9 is the more useful marker for monitoring. The tumor arises from pancreatic ducts, is frequently metastatic at presentation, and has an average survival of about one year after diagnosis. Head tumors cause obstructive jaundice, often with a palpable nontender gallbladder.

explanation_incorrect.A: The specificity relationship is reversed: CEA is the less specific marker, while CA 19-9 is the marker associated with pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
explanation_incorrect.B: CA 125 is primarily used for ovarian cancer, not for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
explanation_incorrect.D: AFP is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma and germ cell tumors, not pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
explanation_incorrect.E: PSA is a prostate cancer marker and is not used to monitor pancreatic cancer.

educationalObjective: CA 19-9 is the tumor marker associated with pancreatic adenocarcinoma, while CEA is less specific.
source: Generated from 9. Gastrointestinal.pdf - Pharmacology: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 72-year-old man asks about his risk factors after being diagnosed with pancreatic adenocarcinoma. He smoked for 30 years and quit 5 years ago, was diagnosed with diabetes 4 years ago, and has had chronic pancreatitis for 22 years. His brother also had pancreatic cancer.
question: Which of the following is the strongest risk factor for this malignancy?

options.text: Chronic pancreatitis of more than 20 years' duration
Tobacco smoking
Diabetes mellitus
Age older than 50 years
Family history of pancreatic cancer in a first-degree relative

explanation_correct: Risk factors for pancreatic adenocarcinoma include tobacco smoking, which is the strongest, as well as chronic pancreatitis especially when present for more than 20 years, diabetes, and age older than 50 years. This patient has several of these, but his 30-pack-year smoking history is the most important. The tumor is typically a very aggressive ductal malignancy, often metastatic at presentation, with an average survival near one year after diagnosis. Head tumors cause obstructive jaundice and are associated with CA 19-9 and activating KRAS mutations.

explanation_incorrect.A: Chronic pancreatitis of more than 20 years is an important risk factor, but First Aid identifies tobacco smoking as the strongest single risk factor.
explanation_incorrect.C: Diabetes is a recognized risk factor and can also be an early manifestation of the tumor, but it is weaker than smoking.
explanation_incorrect.D: Age older than 50 years raises incidence but is not the strongest risk factor compared with tobacco exposure.
explanation_incorrect.E: A family history increases risk, but the listed strongest risk factor is tobacco smoking.

educationalObjective: Tobacco smoking is the strongest risk factor for pancreatic adenocarcinoma, ahead of long-standing chronic pancreatitis, diabetes, and age over 50.
